title: Herpetic Meningoencephalitis Complicating the Resection of a Vestibular Schwannoma: A Case Report
case_prompt:
A 58-year-old woman with active tobacco use and depression underwent complete resection of a right vestibular schwannoma via a translabyrinthine approach. The tumor was classified as Koos stage III and lay in close proximity to the trigeminal nerve. The 9-hour procedure was uneventful. Upon awakening, she had grade II peripheral facial paralysis, right-sided nystagmus, and mild dizziness but was otherwise neurologically intact.

From postoperative day 1 to day 4 she experienced moderate headaches and balance disturbances. On day 5 she developed severe headache and fever of 38.3°C. Neurological examination was unchanged except for persistent nystagmus and facial paralysis; the surgical incision was clean. Chest radiograph, urinalysis, and blood cultures were all negative. Laboratory studies showed lymphocytosis (11,000/mm3) and an elevated C-reactive protein level (32 mg/L).

On day 7 her fever persisted at 38.6°C and inflammatory markers rose further. A noncontrast brain CT scan showed no abscess or venous thrombosis. Lumbar puncture revealed 4,230 erythrocytes/mm3, 50 lymphocytes/mm3, a protein level of 2.09 g/L, a glucose level of 0.23 g/L, lactate 673 mg/L, and no organisms on direct microscopy. Empirical intravenous cefotaxime and vancomycin were initiated.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Aseptic meningitis was considered because of the timing after neurosurgery — “other possibilities, such as aseptic meningitis (common after neurosurgery) … were also considered.”  
2. Decapitated bacterial meningitis was considered as a cause of sterile CSF after antibiotics — “other possibilities, such as … decapitated bacterial meningitis … were also considered.”  
3. Drug-induced meningitis was considered given postoperative medications — “other possibilities, such as … drug‐induced meningitis … were also considered.”  
4. Intracranial abscess or venous thrombosis was excluded by imaging — “a brain CT scan then showed no signs of abscess or venous thrombosis.”  
5. Bacterial meningitis was deemed unlikely given the absence of organisms on CSF microscopy — “no bacteria were observed on direct examination.”  
6. Other viral infections were excluded by a negative CSF PCR panel — “viral PCR testing of the CSF returned positive for HSV‐1 and negative for other viruses (HSV‐2, CMV, enterovirus, HHV‐6, parechovirus, VZV).”
